sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe record retention concepts, distinguishing state record retention laws from the federal HIPAA six-year documentation requirement.
- Explain a patient's HIPAA rights to inspect, obtain copies of, and request amendments to their own health records.
- Recognize when a written authorization is required to release protected health information and apply the minimum necessary standard.
- Apply safe storage and disposal practices for paper and electronic protected health information.
- Flag state-law and office-policy dependence in retention and release decisions and escalate when in doubt.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

HIPAA is like the rules about privacy, not about how long to keep the folder. How long you keep the folder is decided by each state, the way each state sets its own rules for things like driving.

### Question 2

Think of it like keeping a signed permission slip in a safe folder for six years so you can prove later that you had permission.

### Question 3

The length of time to keep a patient's file is decided by the rules of the state where the office is, plus any promises the office made to insurance companies, not by any one big national number.

### Question 4

Just like each state decides its own speed limits, each state decides how long a doctor's office must keep medical files.

### Question 5

When two rules ask for different amounts, the safe choice is to do the one that asks for more, so you satisfy both rules at once.

### Question 6

The six-year rule is about keeping the office's paperwork that proves privacy was handled correctly, not about every single test result in a patient's chart.

### Question 7

Keeping a file only for the shortest allowed time is risky, like throwing away receipts the moment the store's policy allows even though you might still need them for a warranty claim.

### Question 8

A statute of limitations is like a timer for how long someone can complain; you want to keep your proof until the timer runs out.

### Question 9

Because a child cannot bring a lawsuit on their own until they grow up, the countdown to keep their file often does not start until they become an adult.

### Question 10

When a store closes, it still has to keep important customer records safe and tell people how to get them, not just dump everything in the trash.

### Question 11

Active files are like the papers on your desk you use every day, while archived files are like boxes in the storage room you keep for a while before you can throw them out.

### Question 12

A written policy is like a class schedule everyone agrees to follow so nobody accidentally throws away something important too soon.

### Question 13

The state rule is about how long to keep the patient's actual chart, while the HIPAA six-year rule is about how long to keep the office's privacy paperwork, like two different boxes with different timers.

### Question 14

Some states treat pictures like X-rays as special items that must be kept even longer than the written chart, like keeping the original photo along with the notes.

### Question 15

The format does not change the rule: a picture of your file saved on a computer has to be kept just as long as the paper copy.

### Question 16

The timer for how long to keep a file starts from the last time the patient came in and new notes were added, not from when they were born.

### Question 17

Sometimes a promise the office made to an insurance company says to keep files even longer than the state requires, like a warranty that asks you to keep the receipt longer than the store's normal rule.

### Question 18

Keeping track of when files can be thrown away is a team job, like everyone in a family helping sort out which old papers are safe to recycle.

### Question 19

Before throwing away old files, you write down what you threw away and when, like keeping a checklist so nobody can say you did it carelessly.

### Question 20

Keeping files is like keeping your medical history safe so the doctor, the billing office, and the courts can all find what they need if something comes up later.

### Question 21

Patients have the right to see and get a copy of their own medical file, just like you have the right to see your own report card, but not anyone else's.

### Question 22

The office has about a month to get the file ready, and it may ask for one extra month if it gives a written note explaining why.

### Question 23

The office can charge a fair price to cover paper, postage, and the work of making the copy, like paying for copies at a copy shop, but it should not add on hidden charges.

### Question 24

If your file is already on a computer, the office should give you a computer copy if it is easy to make, not insist on paper.

### Question 25

If your report card has a wrong grade, you can ask the school to fix it through the proper process, but you cannot just erase and rewrite it yourself.

### Question 26

A patient can ask the office to be extra careful about who sees their health details, like asking a friend to keep a secret from certain people.

### Question 27

A patient can ask the office to call a different, more private number, just like asking a friend to text instead of calling the house phone.

### Question 28

It is like asking the office for a log of who they shared your file with, but they do not have to list the routine sharing they did to treat you or bill for your care.

### Question 29

A parent usually has the right to see their child's file, the way a parent can see a child's report card, unless a special rule says otherwise.

### Question 30

Notes a therapist writes for their own memory are kept extra private, like a diary, and are not simply handed over with the rest of the chart.

### Question 31

Most of your file you can see, but notes gathered specifically to get ready for a lawsuit are kept separate, like a lawyer's private prep folder.

### Question 32

Just like a bank checks your ID before giving out your money, the office checks who you are before giving out your health information.

### Question 33

Even when someone is in a hurry, the office still checks ID and follows the process, like an airport checking your boarding pass before you board.

### Question 34

When someone passes away, the person officially in charge of their affairs, like an executor, is the one who can ask for their records, not just anyone.

### Question 35

The office can say no only in very special situations, like when seeing the file could cause real harm, and even then the patient can ask a second doctor to double-check.

### Question 36

A patient can choose to just look at their file, like reading your own report card without needing to make a photocopy of it.

### Question 37

Even if a patient owes money, the office still has to give them a copy of their own file, just like a library cannot keep your book forever over a small fine.

### Question 38

The assistant's job is like a librarian who checks your card and fetches the book; if something unusual comes up, they call the manager instead of deciding alone.

### Question 39

The office can charge for the paper and the work of making copies, but not for the time spent hunting through the filing cabinet to find the file.

### Question 40

The owner of a file can always look at their own file, but a stranger or a lawyer has to show a signed permission slip to see it.

### Question 41

The office needs a signed permission slip only for sharing that is not part of the normal treating-and-billing routine, like sending your file to a life insurance company.

### Question 42

When your doctor sends your file to the specialist you were sent to, no extra permission slip is needed because it is part of taking care of you.

### Question 43

A permission slip has to say exactly what is being shared, who is sharing it, who gets it, and when it expires, like a field-trip form with all the blanks filled in.

### Question 44

After the 'use by' date on a permission slip passes, the office needs a fresh permission slip before sharing anything new.

### Question 45

You can always change your mind about a permission slip, as long as the office has not already sent your information out.

### Question 46

Before telling a relative about someone's health, the office checks whether the patient said it is okay, like asking before sharing a friend's news.

### Question 47

A subpoena is like an official letter from a court asking for the file, and the office follows its rulebook and asks a lawyer to be sure before handing anything over.

### Question 48

Some sharing is required by law to keep people safe, like telling health officials about a contagious illness, and that sharing does not need a permission slip.

### Question 49

Share only the smallest slice of information needed to get the job done, like giving someone just the page they need instead of the whole book.

### Question 50

For a child's records, the parent or guardian signs the permission slip, just like a parent signs a child's field-trip form.

### Question 51

A spouse asking on the phone still needs to show the office that the patient gave permission, like needing a signed note before picking up someone else's package.

### Question 52

A life insurance company asking for your file is not the same as a doctor or your health plan, so the office needs your signed permission slip first.

### Question 53

Therapy notes are like a private diary that needs its own special permission slip, not just the regular one, before they can be shared.

### Question 54

The office cannot sell a list of patients to a marketing company without each patient's signed permission, like not sharing a class roster without asking everyone first.

### Question 55

The office cannot sell your health file for money without your written permission, just like a store cannot sell your personal information without asking.

### Question 56

Sending a fax is like mailing a letter: you double-check the address, put the right envelope on it, and make sure it got to the right mailbox.

### Question 57

The log is like a sign-out sheet for your file that shows who borrowed it, when, and with whose permission.

### Question 58

A permission slip has to be written down and signed, not just said out loud or guessed from someone staying quiet.

### Question 59

Sharing with another doctor for your care is allowed, but the office still sends only the parts that doctor needs, not the whole cabinet.

### Question 60

If someone is too sick to speak for themselves, the doctor or office can share the important details with the family when that is clearly what is best for the patient.

### Question 61

Paper records are kept in locked cabinets, like keeping important papers in a locked drawer so only the right people can open it.

### Question 62

To get rid of papers with private information, you shred them into tiny pieces so nobody can put them back together, like shredding an old credit card statement.

### Question 63

Deleting a file is like erasing a pencil mark that can still be seen; the office has to use special tools that make the data truly unreadable before getting rid of a hard drive.

### Question 64

Before giving away an old computer or copier, the office must wipe its memory clean, like erasing a whiteboard before passing it to someone else.

### Question 65

Protecting computer health information needs three kinds of help working together: rules and training (administrative), locks and doors (physical), and passwords and encryption (technical).

### Question 66

Each person gets their own key (password) to the computer and locks the screen when they walk away, like locking your bike when you park it.

### Question 67

Keep the computer screen turned away from the waiting room and lock it when you leave, like turning your test paper over so the person next to you cannot see it.

### Question 68

Protected health information is anything that can point to a specific person and their health, like a name plus a diagnosis, but not a general health pamphlet.

### Question 69

A breach is like a real break-in where your private information actually got out, such as a laptop full of records being stolen, rather than a small accidental glimpse.

### Question 70

Sending private health information by normal email is like mailing a secret in a clear envelope; the office must use a secure, locked method instead.

### Question 71

Records stored away from the office are still locked up and kept track of, like valuables kept in a secure storage unit with a log of who goes in.

### Question 72

Copiers secretly remember everything they copy, so before getting rid of one the office must wipe that memory, like clearing photos off an old phone before selling it.

### Question 73

Writing down what was shredded and when is like keeping a receipt for recycling old papers, so you can prove you handled them properly.

### Question 74

Automatic logoff is like a screen that locks itself when you leave, the way a tablet locks after you stop using it.

### Question 75

No matter whether it is paper or computer files, getting rid of private health information means making it impossible to read again, like shredding paper into unreadable bits or erasing a memory completely.
